GREENSBORO, N. C., June 24.—The lynching of the two men a few days since in Stokes County for rape, and the lynching of another one two weeks ago, does not seem to have had the effect looked for by the lynchers. This morning as Lizzie Fluch, a little 10-year-old daughter of Mrs. Jennie Fluch, living near Hillsboro, was on her way to the spring, she was accosted by William Gauch, a negro of bad character. The second made an infamous proposal to the girl, who, frightened by the look in his eyes, attempted to run away. He caught her and committed a rape upon her person. He at once died, and the child now lies in a precarious condition. Citizens of the county are looking for him.

Intelligence has reached here also of an infamous offense of a similar nature at Martinsville yesterday evening. Charles Gilmor, a negro, actually went into the house of Mr. Prince Winchester, white he and his wife were absent. The sole occupant of the house at the time was Miss Winchester. Knowing Gilmor, she asked him what he wanted, and suspecting that he had crept into the house for the purpose of robbery, she ordered him out. The negro, glaring boldly at her, told her he had no idea of leaving yet, and then went on to tell her to keep quiet on pain of death. At once guessing his horrible design, the young woman began to scream for help. Gilmor attempted to commit his devilish design upon her person, and despite her great struggles would have accomplished his purpose had he not been frightened off by the sound of footsteps of neighbors attracted by the girl's screams. He barely had time to leap from the rear window before they entered the house. Posses of citizens have been hunting him all day. This is the third offense of this character committed by Gilmor. Once he was convicted of an attempt at rape and sentenced to nine years in the Penitentiary, but his counsel succeeded in having his sentence shortened. He was a few years after convicted of rape and sentenced to twenty years in the Penitentiary, but after serving nine years he was released.

IN MEMORIAM.
Death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer—Meeting of the Official Board of Tryon Street Church, Charlotte.

The recent death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer, late of Edenton Street Church, Raleigh, former pastor of Tryon Street Charlotte, has affected the hearts of his former charge with deepest sorrow, and is felt in the whole community. During his pastoral charge of Tryon Street Church, through a period of four years, his ministry was marked by gentleness, faithfulness and ability—the most perfect esteem, affection, and confidence of his flock was maintained, while not a single discord occurred to mar the harmony of the relation between pastor and people.

The impress that he left upon this community was only for good. The fervency of his piety, the purity of, and transparency of his character, the simplicity and geniality of his social life, and the attractiveness of his preaching made him a general favorite in his own Church and won the admiration and esteem of the community.

Richly endowed with these qualities, he was prepared to be a "workman that need not be ashamed"—a faithful shepherd to those "over whom the Holy Ghost made him overseer"—a "wise master-builder" in the temple of the Lord—attractive and loving in the social circle, patient toward the erring, kind and tender in the sick room and house of mourning.

Deeply impressed with his character, we are deeply affected by his early death. We feel that we and the whole Church have suffered a great loss. We feel that the grief of his family is our grief, and the grief of the Church.

Hence, as we are bowed with a common sorrow, we mingle our tears with theirs. While wife, and father, and mother, and child, sit solitary in the shadow of this great grief, our hearts not only feel a kindred pang, but respond in sympathy and condolence to the appeal that comes from bleeding hearts.

Again we are impressed with the inscrutable mystery of Providence in removing a life so full of promise to the Church, just as it was approximating its prime, while there are so many waste places uncultivated and harvests ungathered. The workmen fall, still work goes on. The soldier dies at his post, still the battle does not cease; nor are the banners furled. "God buries His workmen, but carries on His work." So is it ever. We reverence this wisdom. We bow to this power. We adore this goodness. We are subdued under a sense of infinity!

While we stand with uncovered head in the presence of the Disposer of events, and bow our hearts in profoundest grief, we recognize in it the special providence of God, who is "too wise to err and too good to be unkind." Thus endeavoring to submit to the supreme decision of the Head of the Church, and to acquiesce in all the developments of His providence, we, the officers of Tryon Street Church, representing in this case the sentiments of the whole Church, while expressing our own sorrow at the death of our former pastor and friend, desire most heartily and sincerely to express to the bereaved family of the deceased our deepest sympathy; and we do most devoutly pray that God, in whose service he lived, labored, and died, may communicate to them His richest consolations in this trying hour, and so sanctify this afflictive dispensation of His providence as that it shall prove to them a blessing, both for time and eternity.

It was ordered that this communication be sent to the Charlotte papers and Raleigh Christian Advocate for publication—also that a copy be sent to Mrs. A. A. Boshamer as a testimony of our sympathy and affectionate regard.

OFFICIAL BOARD.
Charlotte, N. C., Oct. 13, 1881.

Local Items.

There have been fine rains in this section this week, greatly encouraging farmers in their small-grain work. While there have been killing frosts in the central part of the State two weeks ago, vegetation about here has scarcely been nipped or colored by frost.

A workman, W. A. Sing, in Mr. Josiah Asbury's planing mill, had his hand nearly severed from the wrist by a buzz saw. The saw caught his wrist band which drew the arm also. He will be detained from work some time.

The Almanac sellers or drummers on the streets are about as big a nuisance as the boot-blacks in New York.

Considering the very dry and hot Summer and Fall, the health of Charlotte has been remarkably good, equal to any Mountain city or town.

Sheriff Mays, of Alexander county, considering it unsafe to keep the murderer of Miss Thompson, E. H. Dockery, in the Alexander jail, or even in the jail of any adjoining county, brought the prisoner to this city to be committed to jail here. It was through Dockery's confession that Church, one of the murderers, was lynched, and it is thought his testimony in Court will seriously implicate two others. One, Adams, is under bond to appear at Court now. Evidently it was the friends of these that lynched Church.

The notorious female Minstrels are advertised to appear in Wilmington at an early day. There is an Ordinance in this city against permitting such vulgar performances in the Opera House or elsewhere in Charlotte.

The Hornet's Nest Riflemen of this city, about 30 in number, went to the Yorktown Centennial celebration, under command of E. F. Young.

In Jackson Township, Union county, resided an aged widow lady, Mrs. Godfrey, with her daughter and a small negro boy as servant. On Sunday morning last Mrs. Godfrey was awakened by cries from her daughter, who slept in an adjoining room; being old and feeble she could not herself render any assistance, but sent the boy to the house of a colored man near by. On the arrival of the man the scoundrel ran out and escaped in the darkness. He found that Miss Godfrey had been outraged and choked to stifle her cries. There were found a stick and wagon hammer. The former was identified by a colored man as one he had seen in the possession of Edmund Davis, negro and ex-convict. A party of men in the neighborhood followed and captured the negro eight miles from Mrs. Godfrey's house. He was brought back to Union and taken before Miss Godfrey—but she could not identify him as the room was dark. He was placed in jail where he soon confessed the crime. When it became known a party of three hundred men, one hundred of whom were blacks, took him and hung him to a tree near the scene of the crime. After the crowd was satisfied he was dead they dispersed, leaving the fiend hanging. The party was composed of the best citizens of Union county, and many of the black people insisted he should be burned. Miss Godfrey is 35 years of age, of unblemished character and her condition is quite critical, as she was seriously hurt. The negro was indifferent and said he was willing to be hung. We are glad his request was carried out.

A Sensation in Colorado—Murder and Suicide.

LEADVILLE, December 4th.—Gold Park mining camp is in a furure of excitement. Four days ago Henry Weston, foreman of the Gold Park Mining Company, was shot and killed by one Bagley, a discharged blacksmith. Bagley also made an unsuccessful attempt to shoot Superintendent Turney. He then fortified himself in a cabin, which was immediately surrounded by a mob. The cabin was beigeed for eight hours without dislodging the occupant. Finally a large quantity of giant powder was placed near the door and ignited. The explosion following tore the cabin to pieces, and Bagley was found with a bullet hole through his heart, having evidently committed suicide. Bagley has several sympathizers, who have threatened Turney's life, and a strong guard surrounds his cabin day and night. Jack White and Bagley's friends were ordered out of the camp by the Vigilantes, and paraded the town all day with a pair of cocked revolvers looking for the committee, but left at night. Much trouble is anticipated.

Repenting at Leisure.

NEW YORK, December 3d.—The evening papers have the following: About two years ago the daughter of Amos Stillman, of Brooklyn, eloped with W. S. Guild. Miss Stillman was only about 16, while Guild was 70. After a private marriage ceremony, they slipped away to Europa without the knowledge of relations or friends. Things were not just what the young bride thought they would be, and in four days she became home-sick and prevailed upon Guild to return. When they reached the wharf in New York he hired a coach and sent her home to her parents, while he got upon another steamer and set sail for California. For one year he remitted the young bride $10 per week, and then the remittance stopped. Now she sues him for a limited divorce on the ground of abandonment. It is understood that he claims she abandoned him. This morning a motion was made by her counsel for counsel fees and alimony. It was opposed by the counsel for defendant, who said his client was in California, and he would have to send affidavits to him. The case was postponed.

A Bold Bond Robbery.

CLEVELAND (O.), December 31.—A daring theft captured a box from the Commercial National Bank, containing $117,000 in bonds. They were Milwaukee and St. Paul Railroad, Chicago and Milwaukee Railroad, Chicago and Atchison Bridge Company bonds. The man had been sitting in the office, and when the coupon cutting was finished and the bonds replaced in the box, he quickly whisked the box from the table and disappeared, being gone half an hour before the bonds were missed. President D. P. Eell was responsible for the careless manner in which the securities were exposed. The bonds are all negotiable. The man was short and stout, with short-cropped whiskers.

Fools and Damphools.
The world has agreed for the sake of convenience to divide its fools into two species. One it calls simply a fool; the other, to adopt the word which Doesticks applied to his friend, it calls a damphool. This is used strictly in its scientific, not its profane, and has nothing in common with the shallow and random use which angry men make of it to give vent to their momentary irritation. It is as distinct and technical a label as "mustang" to describe a species of horse, or "terrier" to describe a species of dog.

A fool is often harmless, and may be snubbed and kept in order. A damphool cannot be. A fool is often tolerable and docile. If he cannot be taught much wisdom, he can be taught obedience and respect. But though a damphool may have intelligence, he has little or no reverence. A fool may have some humor, but a damphool has none. A tool can be made a fool of; a damphool makes a fool of himself. A fool may have a little sense, but whatever other sense a damphool may possess, he is sure to lack common sense. A fool may be humble and retiring, but it is the essence of his kinsmen to be conceited and self-asserting. A fool generally knows he is a fool, and so is often doleful when he thinks of it; but a damphool never knows it, and so is happy. A fool is often stupid, headless, blundering, aimless, like a hen or a fly; the other is strutting, irritating, conceited, like a turkey and a peacock; or a noisy nuisance, like a June beetle. A fool is often patient, well-digposed, and, though slow, good-natured, like the ass; but his foster brother is apt to bear malice, and is intelligently obstinate like the mule.

To the ranks of the odious kind of fool belong those who hanker morbidly for notoriety—the Tanners, the Bradlaughs, the Guiteaus, the Booths, the Count Johannes and George Francis Trains. Poor Train, however, has stepped down and out of the ranks, and now appears to be simply and only a fool. The fool is an object of sympathy, of pity, compassion and help; his robust relative gives cause for disgust, for sport, for derision and ridicule. Shakspeare, of course, saw the difference between these types, and has drawn them with his usual clearness and acuteness. His fools and clowns are famous—Touchstone and Dogberry; Launce, Slender old Gobbo, and the like; but his damphools—such as Justice Shallow, Pistol, Falstaff, Polonious, old Capulet, have equal rights to consideration. When, in the play of “Midsummer Night’s Dream,” the dramatist changed Bottom the Weaver into an ass, he turned his damphool into a simple fool. For Bottom the Weaver imagines he can write a play, take the chief role and be stage manager all at the same time, making himself poussed and ridiculous, indeed; but changed into an ass he is docile and humble and wants only to have his head scratched and to be fed on dried peas and good sweet hay.

A fool may be pious and reverential, believe in creeds and religion; but the other sort is quite likely to be an atheist. David undoubtedly meant to write that the damphool “hath said there is no God.”

Benjamin Bird (colored), convicted of the murder of Policeman Nelson (colored) June 25, 1880, during the mill riot at Jacksonville, Fla., was executed at 12 o'clock, Friday, in the jail yard. Next foren o1, about 5 o'clock, he called her, but got no answer. He went into her room and found that the whole left side of her was crushed in and marks of violence all over her body. West Virginia and the Mother State.

If there is any one point upon which the people of this State are substantially of one mind it is as to the perpetual separate Stateship of West Virginia. For many years there has not been a single public man, or a journal of any creed or party, that has expressed any inclination for a reunion. Even the border-line feeling in favor of it that was manifested in Greenbrier County just after the close of the War seems to have died out. At least we hear nothing more of it. The sense of a long course of injustice toward the people of West Virginia on the part of the old State, when we were a part of it, is still alive in this State among the older people, outside of any question of politics, and the younger generation have no traditions that are not West Virginian in their character. We are all looking forward hopefully to the day when West Virginia will be developed by railroads and be made one of the most prosperous States of the Union. The more the public know of the resources of West Virginia the more they realize that she has

the elements of a great future as a State. We do not want, therefore, to be hampered by any adverse policy, such as that which kept us back under the old régime, when the public money represented in the debt of Virginia was spent almost exclusively for the development of the territory outside of our borders.

GARRISON'S GRIT.

A Little "Sand" and a Handy Revolver Saved Him a Lynching—His Explanation of the Trouble with the Grangers and His Account of the Fire in the Cheese Factory.

Young Garrison, the Winfield cheesemaker, whose arrest for alleged incendiarism and whose narrow escape from a lynching at the hands of his angry creditors were referred to in a dispatch in yesterday's Tribune, was brought before the Justice of the Peace at Wheaton yesterday, and obtained a continuance until tomorrow. Young Garrison's explanation is that it had been customary to collect money for his patrons and hold it over from time to time, and no trouble had ever come of it until now. The reason he had not paid dividends to the Winfield farmers was that some of his October collections were behind, and he desired to make as large a payment as possible. The claims ranged from $20 to $500, and aggregated several thousand dollars. He had promised his patrons to pay them on Thursday last, and had on hand for that purpose $7,000 in greenbacks. Not desiring to keep this large sum in one place, where burglaries could get it in case they should raid the establishment, he divided it into three parcels, and hid it in a room on the second floor of the factory on Wednesday night. He then, in company with Mr. Frank Burroughs, the young man who was working in the factory, retired. They slept in an adjoining room, on the second floor, in which were their clothes and the books of the concern. CHICAGO, November 28, 1881.
Corruption in. Chicago courts re-
CHICAGO, November 28, 1881.

Corruption in Chicago courts received a death blow to-day at the hands of Judge Tuley, of the criminal bench. He dismissed a whole panel of jurors. Why? Simply because he considered those composing it to be men unworthy to act impartially. He avowed his purpose not to accept as a juror a man not of the highest reputation for integrity. This is a move in the right direction, and Judge Tuley deserves the greatest praise for taking the initiative in this much needed reform; but it is to be hoped that the bench throughout the city, and the whole country, will be influenced to adopt the same salutary measures.

Rowell, the great English pedestrian, is in Chicago. He considers young Dobler, of Chicago, the second best walker in the world. They are matched to walk at no far distant day.

The Pennsylvania railroad has commenced a prosecuting war on the "scalpers." How very strange it is that none of the "scalpers" are ever prosecuted successfully. A friend at my elbow intimates that the several railroads may, periodically, when passenger travel is light and funds short, "unload" tickets to the scalpers. By this dodge persons who could not pay full fare would be induced to buy low priced tickets. Thus an impetus would be given to travel and expenses to rolling stock be paid, while the regular full fare traffic would not be injured. My friend may be right. If so, then this hurrah against the poor scalper is all buncombe.

The Jews of Chicago are organizing for the relief of their brethren who are being driven from Russia, and who are coming to Chicago. This is a praiseworthy move.

The fiend who murdered Mr. Hessler, a German farmer of North Evanson, near Chicago, last week, as mentioned in my last letter to the LEDGER, has been caught and has confessed the crime. His name is John Galus and his age twenty-two. He says he struck his victim with a hatchet because he called him vile names. When he found he had killed him he put on the dead man's clothes, took his money and left the house. He seems very indifferent to his situation, evidently justifying himself for committing the terrible deed on the grounds that the old man drove him into a high passion by applying to him villainous epithets that reflected upon his mother's honor and virtue.

The Irish National Convention, to be held the 30th instant and 1st and 2d proximo, will be a grand affair. Mr. Parnell will be among the distinguished guests of the convention.

The "Elgin Milk Company," of Chicago, has gone up the flue. Let it be known that this appellation is applied to the convenient water pump.

They cite the quick justice meted out to Booth and his associates in the terrible murder of President Lincoln. To your correspondent, the trial of Guiteau appears a miserable farce. It seems strange that the Judge does not compel the proper respect due the bench to be practiced before him. It is an outrage upon decency to permit an egotistical fiend to turn the halls of justice into a side-show; and the court that permits such to be done, stands convicted before the people as one lacking that high sense of honor generally looked for in such exalted positions.

ASSASSINATION OF AN OHIO WOMAN.
GORE, O., Dec. 28.—At 6:30 o'clock this evening an unknown man opened the door of the house of Mrs. Manley Terrell, a widow living on the outskirts of this place, and shot her through the heart. Her two grown daughters were in the room at the time, but can give no description of the murderer, the deed being so quickly done and it being dark. He was armed with a revolver which had one empty chamber. Our community was startled and shocked on Tuesday morning last by the rumor, which proved to be founded on fact, that two of the prisoners in the jail had been taken from their cells on the previous night and hanged near the Bayou DeSiard road about two and a half miles from the court-house. These unfortunate parties were Alec Wilson, charged with the murder of Reuben Leonard and Perry Munson, charged with the murder of Anderson Mitchell—these, and their victims were all negroes. Both murders had been cold blooded and premeditated In the first case the victim was shot down at night and the other had his neck broken by a blow from a heavy bludgeon, whilst he was quietly walking on the roadside in company with his wife. In both cases the testimony against the prisoners was circumstantial but quite strong and convincing—still they had neither been proved guilty—and were both held in jail, subject to the investigation and action of the Grand Jury. The idea that our parish or its officers will arrest parties charged with the commission of crime and then fail to protect them is horrifying and revolting in the extreme. That a party of men can come to our parish seat, get possession of the jail keys, and without resistance commit such a crime as has startled our community this week as equally shameful and disgraceful. We trust and believe that the proper officers will investigate this matter to the bottom and make an example of all parties in any manner responsible for this barbarously cruel act.

FIGHT WITH MOONSHINERS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

ATLANTA, Ga., June 6.—Deputy United States Marshal Bolton reached Atlanta today with a bullet lodged in his body near his heart, which he received last night about 11 o'clock, in Forsyth County, while he and one or two men were attempting to capture two wagons loaded with "mountain dew." Newton, of the militia who has been sent out by the governor to examine and report upon the situation. Perry County Again to the Front.
Sequel to the late War-An Editor Shot.
A special to the Gazette, dated Morrilton, July 22nd. says: This morning about daylight, a messenger arrived from Perryville after a doctor to attend J. L. W. Matthews, whom, he stated, had been shot.

Some time ago dissatisfaction was expressed as to the way County Judge Harris conducted his court. It was claimed by the enemies of Harris that Matthews had influenced objectionable proceedings, and that together Matthews and Harris were determined to run the affairs of the county. Threats were made, but at first no one was disposed to regard the matter in a serious light. Harris received a notice, telling him to leave the county, and that if he did not leave by a certain day, the extremest of measures would be adopted. Matthews also received notice, but being a very cool, determined man, he paid but little attention to the threat. On the day when the time expired, about twenty armed men rode into Perryville. Harris was holding court at the time, but becoming frightened left the bench hurriedly. Matthews. still cool and collected, walked around town and met the men on the square. They did not speak to him, but rode quietly away. Judge Harris went to Little Rock and called on the governor, the result of which visit has been published. When General Newton went to Perryville everything was quiet, so far as appearances could be taken as evidence. The disturbed and disturbing elements moved around together, and those who expressed a belief that blood would be shed were regarded as sensationalists. Some of the best citizens of the county affirmed that the armed men who had come into town were deer hunters and intended no harm to Matthews or Judge Harris. Gen. Newton's investigation seemed to be very satisfactory, and it is believed here that if his orders had been executed; that if the civil authorities had acted upon his suggestions, the affair would not have had a serious termination.

"What were the circumstances of the killing?" asked your correspondent of the messenger.

"About 9 o'clock last night Matthews and a man who works in the printing office with him went out to the well after water. As they returned, the printer walked a short distance in advance of Matthews. When they reached the house the printer entered, and just as Matthews was about to ascend the steps a gun fired, and Matthews fell. The printer sprang to the door and saw some one running away, but, owing to the darkness, could not identify him. In a moment the town was aroused and greatly excited. An examination showed that eighteen buckshot had taken effect in Matthews' left side and that he was fearfully mutilated. I was immediately dispatched for a surgeon."

Dr. George, who left immediately to attend Matthews has just returned. He reports Matthews dead, and says that the greatest excitement prevails. A notice has been left at Judge Harris' residence, telling him to leave the county immediately. The whole thing is regarded as a feud without political significance. Matthews' record was bad, but since he established the paper at Perryville, he has conducted himself very quietly.

Sheriff Van, of Perry county, has telegraphed for prosecuting attorney Wood to come and investigate the affair. The people here are of the opinion that more forcible means should be adopted.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., July 30.—The desperate condition of affairs in Perry county, in defiance of law and order, has resulted in Gov. Churchill placing it under martial law. Not only has Matthews been assassinated, and old man Harris bulldozed, but the magistrates have been deterred from issuing writs for the perpetrators, a justice of the peace stating he would leave the county before he would become involved in the matter. The bark Ibis, from Pensacola, lay yesterday at the foot of Seventeenth street, North river. A Sun reporter boarded her and asked Captain Sawyer if he had really seen whales off Pimlico Sound on his way up the coast last Saturday.

"Whales?" said the genial Captain, "Any number of them. There must have been two miles of black backs and water-spouts."

Capt. Sawyer unrolled a time-worn chart on the table in his cabin and with his dividers followed down a number of pencil marks to latitude 40 degrees and longitude 74 degrees 15 minutes. This brought him to a point about eighty miles off Pimlico Sound, and further northeast of Cape Hatteras.

"It was on Saturday and Sunday, he continued, "when we encountered these sperm whales going south of southwest, as if to go around Hatteras. They were going very slowly, backs above the water, and were spouting all of the time. They were strolling along in groups, sunning themselves half an hour at a time, and then taking a header and coming up to spout."

"How many were there?"

"Well, first we met two schools of about 100 each, I should say. Occasionally they frolicked and flopped about heavily in a sort of dignified and elephantine sport. More followed, and the next morning (Sunday) we saw more. Altogether there were over 700 on the picnic. We passed within 500 feet of two big fellows, but they seemed preoccupied and didn't notice the ship. I don't think they knew we were there."

"Had you any means of capturing them?"

"No, and it did seem a pity to have so much valuable sperm oil indolently swimming away from us. There were some big whales there, too. I said to Limerick, one of my men here, 'Now there's a fellow that's worth $2000,' and he must have been, and there were bigger ones in the school. It would have been a harvest for a whaling ship. A million dollars in sperm whales is too good a haul to let go by, but we couldn't do anything. Occasionally I have seen a

sperm whale cruising along as far south as Savannah, and once in a while I've heard of whale ships off about there. But I never saw so many whales at one time before anywhere."

"Where were they going?"
"For squids, probably. That's a favorite food with them."

"Is there any danger to be feared from them?"
"No; they're harmless. I think I never heard of more than one case where a whale attacked a vessel, and that's in ancient history. Over a hundred years ago, I believe, the ship Easex was run down by a mad whale. My own experience with whales has been that they are shy, and if they upset a boat, do it by accident in trying to get away."

A Meeting of Dissatisfied Democrats and What Came of It.

Special to the Appeal.]

OXFORD, Miss., July 30.—The dissatisfied element of the Lafayette county Democracy met in mass-meeting here to-day. The crowd numbered about 200, 100 to 125 of whom participated in and approved of the meeting. A new set of delegates were appointed to go to Jackson with instructions to vote against Stone for Governor, and to vote for W. D. Holder for Auditor and E. H. Dial for Secretary of State. This new delegation, of course, will not be recognized by the State Convention.

A Greenback meeting was also held here to-day. An effort was made to get up a fusion with the Republicans, but the Republicans refused to nestle and bolted the meeting.

OKOLONA, MISS.

A Negro Murderer Lynched by a Mob of His Own Color.

OKOLONA, July 30.—About three weeks ago Robert Barker, colored, wilfully murdered Luther White, colored, about four miles from here. Barker went to White's house, and, without any notice or cause whatever, knocked him once or twice in the head with a club, spattering his brains over the floor. The murderer, not satisfied, then took his knife and ripped White's abdomen open. Barker has been at large until yesterday, when he was brought into town by a crowd that had been on the lookout for him ever since he committed the deed, and delivered to the proper authorities. To-day the officer, with a guard, started with him to the county jail in Houston, which is about twenty miles from here. When about six miles from town they were met by an armed mob, who seized the prisoner, carried him a short distance into the woods and shot him dead. Barker pleaded earnestly for his life, but without effect. Justice was meted out to him properly by men of his own color.

INDIAN ATROCITIES.

More Troops Needed to Protect the Frontier Ranchmen.

DENVER, July 30.—The Tribune's Las Vegas letter has the following on good authority: The Indians who attacked two packers near Alama Canon, on the 19th instant, have been followed ever since by Lieutenant Guilfoyle's command, which a day or two since surprised them in camp. After one hour's engagement the Indians fled, leaving the whole camp outfit, two horses and twelve mules in the possession of the soldiers. Two Indians are supposed killed and several wounded but were carried off. The Indians fled toward the Rio Grande, and are supposed to be bound for Old Mexico. They were direct from the Mescala agency, and numbered eleven bucks and one squaw.

Reliable news from Engle reports the burning of a ranche and a number of Mexicans and two unknown miners by the Indians near there.

It is thought there are three bands of Indians prowling about the country, as their signal fires were seen from Engle last night.

A San Marcial, New Mexico, special says two Mexicans and two miners were murdered between San Jose and Fort McCready by Indians, who are supposed to be heading from the Black Range. Company D, Ninth cavalry, has been ordered upon a scout from Ojo Caliente. Chief Name will probably co-operate with Mescaleros if he is aware they are on the war path.

robert-barker-okolona-1881-07-30.A4: Our readers will remember that we published some weeks since an account of the cruel and inhuman murder of Luther White by Rob. Barker. Since the killing of White it seems Barker has been prowling around the neighborhood with the avowed intention of killing three or four other persons. When this was accomplished he proposed to flee the country. On last Friday evening the quiet of the city was disturbed by the entrance of at least one hundred armed men, mostly colored, who had the desperado in charge, and delivered him over to the officers of the law. Barker was at once put in jail and closely guarded on Friday night, and Saturday morning was brought before the Mayor, where he waved an examination, and was committed to jail. The jail here not being secure, Officer Buford was instructed to carry the prisoner to Houston for confinement. Early in the morning a large crowd of people assembled in town, and it was evident much excitement prevailed among them, and some suqdued threats of lynching were made. The officers were aware of this, and knew full well the only safety for the prisoner was to get him out of town immediately, and if possible without the knowledge of the infuriated populace. This they endeavored to do, but the sequel showed without success. The lynchers kept a close lookout, and were fully aware of all the movements made. Indeed it seems that a party of near one hundred stationed themselves on the road about five miles from town, at what is known as Shaw creek bottom and patiently waited the arrival of the posse, while a large number followed the officer and his charge from town. When they arrived at Shaw creek, the signal was given and twenty or thirty colored men jumped into the road and demanded the criminal. Resistance was worse than useless, and Officer Buford could do nothing more than beg for the life of the culprit and enter his protest against the unlawful act. The mob did not parley but seized the bridle of the mule upon which Barker was mounted, hurried him into the thicket, and before the officer could hitch his horse and follow to the place of execution, the report of twenty guns told the fate of the murderer. After the shooting the crowd dispersed as if by magic, and the slayer of three men, was left a lifeless, mangled mass upon the ground. We do not approve of mob law, but there can be no doubt, that the victim in this case received a justly merited punishment, and we trust it may prove a warning deter others as vicious from crime
robert-barker-okolona-1881-07-30.A5: JUDGING from the numerous cases, which have occurred within the past few years, the negro Rob. Barker would have made a saint in glory, if the wicked mob that shot him to death had only given him time to repent and be converted. In other other words, had he been incarcerated in jail, brought to trial and sentenced to expiate his heinous crime on the scaffold, the pious labors of the zealous ministry, who bank so heavily on the historic "thief on the cross," would have converted his dark soul and sent him shouting to the Heavenly paradise. The action of the Lynchers was hard on Barker, but we console ourselves with the reflection that the society of Saints and Angels is not to be contaminated with his presence.
